title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview with Weekly on Stocks on June 28, 2023
summary: In an interview for a Chinese audience, Pabrai reflects on what he has learned from observing Charlie Munger up close: rationality, holding both sides of an argument, studying founders' histories (the BYD/Wang Chuanfu case), being a harsh grader of friends, and surrounding yourself with givers. He shares his views on China, Maotai and Tencent, admits that selling Maotai on Li Lu's advice and selling Ferrari were among his biggest regrets, and advises Chinese investors to buy great businesses at reasonable prices and never sell.

ideas.idea: The most important lessons from Munger came not from what he said but from observing how he interacts with his eight kids, grandchildren, friends and fishing buddy, and how he spends his day.
ideas.detail: Behind the blunt Berkshire-meeting exterior is a warm, loving, rational man who lives simply: Buffett has been in the same home since 1954 (67 years) and Munger in a home he designed since about 1964-65. Books like Poor Charlie's Almanack and Lowenstein's 'The Making of an American Capitalist' cover the rest.

ideas.idea: Buffett gifts about $17,000 a year, the tax-free limit, to roughly 30 family members at Christmas without judging them, while Munger gave half his Berkshire shares to his eight kids in the one year with no estate tax.
ideas.detail: Munger's wife died in the single year the US had no inheritance tax; he split half his Berkshire stock eight ways, about $125M per child then, worth perhaps $500M each today. Many of the children, like Howard Buffett in Ukraine, run foundations, so most of that money will end up improving society.

ideas.idea: Be very rational in business and investing but less rational in relationships, which need emotion; Munger balances the two well.
ideas.detail: At 99, physically declined and no longer playing golf or club bridge, Munger shows no cognitive decline; rationality is central to his success. He is easygoing, eats whatever is served, and the family rations his See's candy to 2-3 times a month, so he gorges at the Berkshire and Daily Journal meetings where no one can stop him.

ideas.idea: You are not entitled to an opinion unless you can state the other side's argument as well as your own; humans become irrational the moment they hold an opinion or ideology.
ideas.detail: He gives Munger's examples of Harvard affirmative action and the Russia-Ukraine war, where one should understand both sides. Holding both sides of an argument in the brain simultaneously is very difficult for most humans.

ideas.idea: Ask five or six competitors which companies in their industry they admire and which are bad; you will quickly learn who is best and worst in ways the numbers do not show.
ideas.detail: A tool both Buffett and Munger use. He warns that falling in love with a company makes rationality go away, and that they study the past carefully to understand how the future will unfold.

ideas.idea: Munger did not buy BYD because Li Lu liked it; he studied Wang Chuanfu's early history and connected him to Edison, Ford and Gates before investing.
ideas.detail: Li Lu's initial BYD investment was almost venture capital. Wang, one of the youngest of 7-8 siblings, was staked by his brother; BYD cut battery costs by making a small glove box clean instead of a whole Japanese-style clean room, and Wang lives in the workers' apartment blocks, creating a culture where people will do anything for him.

ideas.idea: Being rational requires being in alignment, meaning honest and candid with yourself and others, and being a harsh grader of the people you let into your life.
ideas.detail: After meeting someone for the first time he analyses how he feels and sets a high bar: unless truly exceptional, he does not increase the interaction. His father said a good life needs one good wife and one good friend; less is more. Munger's friends, including a humble Minnesota fishing buddy of modest means, were among the highest-quality people he has ever met.

ideas.idea: China's rise under Deng Xiaoping, one of the best leaders any country has had, is the only time the world's largest country lifted so many from extreme poverty to affluence so fast, by unleashing natural entrepreneurs.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He relays Munger's politically incorrect theory that rice cultivation selected for math skill and higher IQ in China, with a downside of a higher propensity to gamble (Macau, Vegas, and stock trading). China's negative population growth is a concern, though not as bad as Korea or Japan.

ideas.idea: China's 1.4 billion people mean a product with broad appeal, especially digital, can scale with tremendous impact, but China is a difficult place for him personally because he does not understand the cultural nuances.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He cites Tencent, Meituan and Pinduoduo as innovations that scaled very fast. When looking at China he asks Li Lu what makes sense; it is easier for people in China to sift through the opportunities than for him.

ideas.idea: Selling Maotai on Li Lu's advice, after Munger ('God') had told him he would still own it when he died, was one of his biggest regrets; it more than doubled after he sold.
ideas.detail: Li Lu suggested Maotai a few years back; Pabrai made 5-6x, then Li Lu called citing distribution/corruption concerns and told him to sell. His daughter ignored the advice and kept her shares. He bought at a tenth of the current price and is now going to take another look.

ideas.idea: Maotai's moat is indestructible: a bottle costs under $5 to make with no automation and unchanged methods for 100 years, yet sells for well over $1,000, economics almost no business on earth has.
ideas.detail: He visited the factory with his daughter and Guy Spier. Even after a recent decline it remains the most valuable liquor company in the world and cannot be touched by any competitor.

ideas.idea: Pony Ma is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of the last 100 years, and Tencent would be at the top of his list in China because of its flexibility and execution, even though the investment has not worked so far.
ideas.detail: He originally owned Alibaba, then switched to Tencent after judging it superior on several fronts. Both have not worked for him, largely due to hard-to-predict government regulation. When restricted in China, Tencent expanded abroad and has excelled at internal R&D, scaling products, investments and partnerships; at ~14x earnings it is reasonably valued, not overvalued.

ideas.idea: The law of large numbers is a real headwind for mega-caps like Tencent and Maotai: it is almost impossible for them to become 10x larger in a few years, so a smaller business can be the better investment.
ideas.detail: Apple hovers around $3 trillion and $4 trillion market caps do not exist; there used to be no businesses above $500-600B. A small pool of capital can find companies that become 10, 20 or 50 times larger, while mega-caps are like aircraft carriers that are hard to navigate.

ideas.idea: Political and regulatory risk in China now warrants a discount that was not a factor a few years ago.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Asked how much discount international capital should demand, he says it is a significant, probably negative factor today that did not exist a few years ago. Being global, he has found good opportunities in Turkey and more recently the US instead.

ideas.idea: To play infinite games, be a giver and surround yourself only with givers; wipe out takers and matchers from your life right away.
ideas.detail: From Adam Grant's 'Give and Take': givers, takers and matchers (who keep score of lunches). Charlie, Warren and all of Charlie's friends are givers who teach without expecting benefit.

ideas.idea: When you find yourself owning a fraction of a great business, pretty much never sell it unless the price is extreme, egregious and crazy.
ideas.detail: His biggest recurring mistake has been selling very good businesses because they appeared overvalued. Ferrari, bought in 2012 via a company that owned it at an effective price under $15, is now over $300 (20x+ in 11 years); selling Ferrari and Maotai, both iconic one-of-a-kind companies, are among his biggest regrets despite making a lot of money on both.

ideas.idea: Keep the calendar empty, as Buffett does, so there is time to think, read and explore; freedom of time is one of the biggest luxuries.
ideas.detail: This interview was the only item on his schedule that day. With nothing scheduled he spent the last few months studying two companies, talking to many people and reading widely until a picture formed.

ideas.idea: Chinese investors' high math skills lead to too much gambling and trading in the stock market; instead study businesses, find the great ones, buy them at reasonable prices and never ever sell them.
ideas.detail: His closing advice to Chinese readers, echoing his Maotai and Ferrari regrets.
